titles.title: LROT: ligand-receptor-guided optimal transport for spatial transcriptomics slice alignment

descriptions.description: Reference implementation of LROT, which embeds a ligand-receptor communication prior as a third cost channel in an entropy-regularised fused Gromov-Wasserstein framework for spatial transcriptomics section alignment, together with the scripts and intermediate results needed to reproduce the figures of the paper.
If you use this software, please cite the paper and this archived release.

affiliation: The Garvan Institute of Medical Research

descriptions.description:
This work should be publicly available by December 2026, please check Zenodo again then

This dataset contains preprocessed spatial transcriptomics data (AnnData and SpatialData objects), pathology annotations, and cell type mapping results from a study profiling tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and high endothelial venules (HEVs) in breast cancer using three spatial platforms: Visium, Visium HD, and Xenium.

Dataset Overview

Study Design:



32 patient samples (anonymized as P01-P32)

3 spatial transcriptomics platforms:



Visium: 40 samples (33 primary tumor samples (32 patients; P29 processed as two replicate sections), 7 matched lymph nodes)

Visium HD: 4 samples at multiple resolutions (8µm, 16µm, 48µm bins)

Xenium: 6 samples at single-cell resolution




Naming Convention:



Primary tumors: P##_Vis (Visium), P##_HD (Visium HD), P##_Xe5k (Xenium 5K panel)

Lymph nodes: P##_LN_Vis

Replicate sections: P29_Vis_Rep1, P29_Vis_Rep2


File Structure

1. anndata_objects.zip

Preprocessed spatial transcriptomics data stored as AnnData objects (.h5ad format), ready for downstream analysis. These files contain:



Gene expression matrices (normalized and log-transformed)

Spatial coordinates

Low resolution H&E images


Contents:





visium/



40 .h5ad files (one per sample) containing Visium spatial data:



Spatial resolution: 55µm diameter spots

Expression data: ~18,000 genes per sample

Includes: Primary tumor samples (P##_Vis) and lymph node samples (P##_LN_Vis)







visium_hd/



Visium HD data organized by bin size for 4 samples (P26_HD, P27_HD, P29_HD, P32_HD):



square_008um/: 8µm × 8µm square bins

square_016um/: 16µm × 16µm square bins

square_048um/: 48µm × 48µm square bins (comparable to Visium)





Note: The 2µm resolution objects are not included in this record to save space. These objects were not used in the final analysis but can be created from the SpaceRanger outs (see the associated GitHub repo for details).

xenium/



6 .h5ad files (P17_Xe5k, P22_Xe5k, P24_Xe5k, P26_Xe5k, P29_Xe5k, P32_Xe5k):



Single-cell resolution spatial data

Expression data: 5,100 genes (5K base panel + 100 custom genes)

Created from cell-by-gene matrices (not subcellular transcript data)

Contains cell centroid coordinates only (segmentation masks not included)

Coordinate system matches H&E image






2. pathology_annotations.zip

Expert pathologist annotations of tissue compartments at the spot/bin level (CSV format). Each file maps spatial barcodes to tissue annotation labels.

Annotation Categories:



Epithelial: invasive carcinoma, in situ carcinoma, benign proliferation, normal epithelium

Immune: tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS), lymphoid aggregate, lymphocytes present

Stroma: desmoplastic stroma, fibrous stroma, adipose tissue

Additional features: blood vessel, lymphovascular invasion (LVI), calcification, duct secretion, nerve, necrosis, haemorrhage


Contents:





visium/



33 annotation files (one per primary tumor Visium sample):



Format: P##_Vis_pathology_annotations.csv

Columns include spot barcodes and tissue labels

Multi-layer annotations: epithelial, immune, and stromal features annotated separately

single_layer column: Collapsed annotation with one label per spot







visium_hd/



4 annotation files for Visium HD samples:



Format: P##_HD_pathology_annotations.csv

Annotations performed at 8µm bin resolution

Single annotation label per bin







visium_lymph_nodes/



Annotations for 7 lymph node samples (P12, P25, P26, P27, P28, P29, P32):



Three files per sample (two annotation types; germinal center provided in both CSV and GeoJSON):



P##_LN_Vis_tissue_annotations.csv: Lymphoid tissue area annotations

P##_LN_Vis_GC_annotations.csv: Germinal center annotations

P##_LN_Vis_GC_annotations.geojson: Germinal center annotations in GeoJSON format (viewable in QuPath)








Usage Notes:



CSV files can be merged with AnnData objects using barcode/bin IDs as keys

GeoJSON files can be visualized in QuPath by opening the corresponding H&E image and importing the annotation file


3. cell_type_mapping.zip

Cell type predictions for all spatial samples using single-cell reference-based methods. Results are organized by method and annotation granularity level.

Methods:



Deconvolution (cell2location): Estimates cell type abundances per spot/bin for Visium and Visium HD

Label transfer (Tangram): Assigns cell type labels to individual cells for Xenium


Annotation Levels:

Each method provides results at three hierarchical levels matching the reference atlas (see original publication for more details: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-021-00911-1):



major_level/: Broad cell type categories (e.g., T cells)

minor_level/: Intermediate cell type subtypes (e.g., CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells)

subset_level/: Most granular cell type annotations (e.g., CD4+ T-regs, GZMK CD8+ T cells)


deconvolution/visium/



Cell type abundance predictions for 33 Visium primary tumor samples:

Files per level: P##_Vis_{level}_q05_cell_abundance_w_sf.csv



Format: Each row = one spot barcode, columns = cell type abundances

Values: Estimated number of cells per cell type per spot (5th percentile of posterior distribution)




deconvolution/visium_hd/



Cell type abundance predictions for 4 Visium HD samples:



Same structure as Visium deconvolution

Performed at two resolutions:



48µm bins (comparable to Visium spots)

16µm bins (higher resolution)



Files: P##_HD_{level}_q05_cell_abundance_w_sf.csv




label_transfer/xenium/



Cell type predictions for 6 Xenium samples:



Files per level: P##_Xe5k_{level}_pred_cell_types.csv

Format: Each row = one cell barcode, columns include predicted cell type labels and confidence scores

Method: Tangram label transfer maps single-cell reference annotations to Xenium cells based on gene expression similarity




Usage Notes:



Deconvolution results can be joined to AnnData .obs using spot/bin barcodes

Label transfer results can be joined to Xenium AnnData .obs using cell barcodes

Choose annotation level based on analysis needs


4. spatialdata_objects.zip

SpatialData objects for Xenium samples (.zip format within the main archive). These contain comprehensive spatial data including subcellular transcript positions, cell segmentation boundaries, and metadata - providing access to the full resolution of Xenium data beyond the aggregated cell-level counts in the AnnData objects.

Contents:



xenium/



6 SpatialData objects (P17_Xe5k, P22_Xe5k, P24_Xe5k, P26_Xe5k, P29_Xe5k, P32_Xe5k):



Transcript-level spatial data with (x, y) coordinates for each detected molecule

Cell and nucleus segmentation boundaries (polygon geometries)

Cell metadata and expression quantification

Coordinates transformed to align with cropped H&E images

Enables analysis of subcellular spatial patterns and transcript distributions

Note: Morphology images are not included in these objects






About SpatialData:

SpatialData is a data framework for integrated analysis of multi-modal spatial omics data, designed to handle diverse spatial elements including points (transcripts), shapes (cell boundaries), and images. It provides a unified interface for working with spatial data at multiple scales.

Usage Notes:



Each sample is stored as a .zip file that must be unzipped before reading. Unpacks into .zarr data.

Compatible with Python spatialdata library (use sd.read_zarr() for reading)

Complements the cell-level AnnData objects by providing full spatial resolution data

Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

titles.title: The Science Behind Squalene: The Human Antioxidant (The Conceptual Source of Stem Cell Niche Defense and Adaptive Altruism Research)

descriptions.description:
Squalene is an isoprenoid antioxidant present in human skin, and a precursor of cholesterol. Squalene is an ancient antioxidant that layers the cell membranes of primitive life form such as archea and cynobacteria. Twenty six years ago, I focussed on Squalene metabolism, as I was interested in primitive oxidative stress and cancer. Initially, a draft on oxidative stress and cancer, written during my clinical practice in Assam and Bhutan during 1994-1998, and as a part of my first research project, the project evolved rapidly during 1999-2000, when Mr. Dieter Beer proposed to write a book on Squalene dietary supplement to expand the dietary supplement markets. I took that opportunity and funding to make an indepth review on adaptive mechanisms against oxidative stress and metabolic stress. 

First published in August 2000, The Science Behind Squalene was not fundamentally a book about squalene; it was an investigation into whether evolutionarily conserved anti-oxidant metabolic networks constitute the first adaptive defense mechanisms by which living systems preserve biological organization under environmental stress.

The monograph outlines the biophysical, cellular and evolutionary foundations of squalene as an endogenous isoprenoid antioxidant. Its "Force of Disequilibrium" U-tube model (Figure 36, p. 140) provides an early theoretical framework for how living systems expend energy continuously to maintain non-equilibrium steady states rather than relaxing toward equilibrium. The chapter "Metabolic Stress and Chaos" proposed that antioxidant defense operates through nonlinear adaptive mechanisms maintaining an organized state of disequilibrium until critical stress thresholds are exceeded, beyond which the compensatory mechanism fails through positive feedback. Written before complex adaptive systems became widely applied in systems biology, this framework anticipated concepts now associated with resilience, nonlinear dynamics, threshold behaviour and adaptive biological organization.

Figure 14 (p. 52) presents the evolution of immune defense from ancestral stem cells under evolutionary pressure; the stem-cell niche-defense reading of this material developed subsequently.

A single clause on p. 12 notes that amaranth is a symbol of avatar kosha in tantric tradition — the only trace in the published text of a larger body of material on Vedic Jiva Upakara Cikitsha Tantra (https://doi.org/10.5040/9798216171232.0007) that was removed before publication.

Together, these early models established the biophysical and heuristic foundation for what later evolved over a 25-year research program into Stem Cell Niche Defense, Altruistic Stem Cells (ASCs), Tumor Stemness Defense (TSD), and the broader systems-biology framework of Adaptive Altruism.

Inspired by the Avatar Kosha of Vedic Altruism, Adaptive Altruism is proposed as a biological theory of transient enhanced-fitness altruism of stem cell niche defense. It is defined as a non-genetic stress-response program wherein actor stem cells utilize an active force of disequilibrium to initially gain metabolic fitness and robustness, execute collective niche protection from a position of strength, and subsequently undergo terminal self-elimination (Adaptive Altruism: scientific translation of Vedic Altruism, p. 11. https://zenodo.org/records/8062404). Beyond immediate cytoprotection, the adaptive-altruistic episode may generate persistent biological information that contributes to the emergence, maintenance, or reconstruction of biological self-identity.

The book should therefore be read not simply as a monograph on squalene, but as an early conceptual foundation for later work investigating how complex adaptive biological systems preserve and reconstruct their organizational identity under stress.

 

Commentary on the book: 

(During the twenty-sixth anniversary of The Science Behind Squalene, a commemorative lecture entitled "From Stem Cell Altruism to Tumor Self-Identity: Rethinking Cancer as a Cooperative System" was delivered at Assam DownTown University in February 2026. Preparing that lecture prompted a comprehensive re-examination of nearly three decades of clinical observations, experimental investigations, and conceptual development, and a need to write a commentary about this book, especially the last chapter, Metabolic Stress and Chaos.  This realization provided the immediate motivation to write a commentary on the book. This is the concept note of the future commentary)

Twenty-Six Years Later: From Adaptive Mechanism of Metabolic Stress  Response to Adaptive Altruism

When The Science Behind Squalene was first published in 2000, it was presented as a scientific exploration of squalene biology, antioxidant defense, metabolic stress, and environmental adaptation. Although centered on a naturally occurring isoprenoid molecule, the book was never intended to be merely a discussion of nutritional supplementation. Rather, it sought to address a broader biological question that had emerged from earlier clinical observations in community oncology: How do living systems preserve themselves under conditions of stress?

Looking back twenty-six years later, it has become apparent that many of the concepts introduced in the book—including adaptive metabolic mechanisms, organized disequilibrium, nonlinear biological organization, stress thresholds, evolutionary adaptation, and endogenous defense systems—represented the earliest formulation of a research programme that subsequently expanded far beyond antioxidant biology. Over the following decades, experimental investigations in hypoxia, stem-cell biology, cancer stem cells, mesenchymal stromal cells, host–pathogen interactions, and tumor microenvironment research progressively transformed these initial concepts into the hypotheses of Stem Cell Niche Defense, the Tumor Stemness Switch, Altruistic Stem Cells, Tumor Stemness Defense, and, most recently, Adaptive Altruism.

This commentary does not seek to reinterpret the original book through hindsight or to claim that later discoveries were already established in 2000. On the contrary, the original text is preserved exactly as it was written. The purpose of the present commentary is to place the book within its historical scientific context by explaining how its central questions evolved through subsequent experimental investigation. Where appropriate, annotations identify concepts that were later supported experimentally, concepts that evolved into new hypotheses, and ideas that remain speculative and require further validation.

 Revisiting the book in light of nearly three decades of research revealed that apparently diverse studies—including antioxidant metabolism, oxidative stress, hypoxia, stem-cell biology, tumor stemness, mesenchymal stromal cell reprogramming, microbial persistence, and community oncology—were not isolated investigations, but successive stages of a single evolving scientific programme. Each addressed different aspects of one overarching systems-level question: How do complex adaptive systems preserve and reconstruct their organizational self-identity under condition of stress?

Adaptive Altruism is proposed as one experimentally grounded, yet still evolving, framework through which this question can now be investigated.

Seen from this perspective, The Science Behind Squalene can be understood as the first conceptual foundation of that programme. The focus of the book was adaptive metabolism; subsequent work expanded this framework to stem-cell biology, tumor biology, and systems medicine. The central scientific question, however, remained remarkably consistent.

Adaptive Altruism, as discussed below and elsewhere, should therefore be regarded not as a departure from the ideas presented in the book, but as their current conceptual synthesis based on twenty-five years of additional experimental evidence.

This commentary is offered in the spirit of scientific continuity. It documents the evolution of ideas rather than their finality, distinguishing historical inspiration from experimental evidence, and established observations from hypothesis-driven interpretation. It is hoped that these annotations will help readers appreciate not only the historical significance of the original book, but also the iterative nature of scientific discovery, in which clinical observation, conceptual reasoning, experimental investigation, and continual revision together shape the emergence of new scientific frameworks.

Adaptive Altruism and the Preservation of Self-Identity in Complex Adaptive Systems

One of the central ideas emerging from The Science Behind Squalene was that biological stress does not arise simply from exposure to environmental injury, but from the failure of adaptive mechanisms responsible for maintaining an organized state of biological disequilibrium. The book proposed that antioxidant defense represents a dynamic, nonlinear process in which living systems continuously adjust their metabolic organization to preserve function under changing environmental conditions. Concepts such as adaptive metabolic responses, organized disequilibrium, stress thresholds, and nonlinear biological organization anticipated a systems-level view of biological resilience, although the terminology of "complex adaptive systems" was not employed at that time.

Over the subsequent twenty-five years, experimental investigations progressively expanded this conceptual framework from metabolism to stem-cell biology, cancer biology, and host-pathogen interactions. Studies of hypoxia revealed that severe stress induces transient stemness through MYC-HIF-2α signalling, enabling subsets of stem cells and cancer stem cells to enter reversible stress-adaptive states. Subsequent work identified altruistic stem cells (ASCs) capable of protecting neighbouring cells through cytoprotective secretory programmes in the lung and BM niches, while later studies demonstrated that tumour-derived signals reprogram mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into Mesenchymal Altruistic Stem Cells (M-ASCs), establishing stem cell niche memory within the tumour microenvironment. More recently, the Tumor Stemness Defense (TSD) phenotype was proposed to explain how hypoxic cancer stem cells (CSCs) may transiently adopt niche-supportive functions that preserve dormant cancer stem-cell reservoirs and facilitate tumour recurrence through the CSC reawakening process. Collectively, these findings support the broader concept that stress adaptation is not exclusively cell-autonomous but may involve transient cooperative interactions that preserve the organization of the larger cellular ecosystem.

These experimental observations have led to the formulation of Adaptive Altruism as a systems-level hypothesis. Rather than describing altruism in the classical evolutionary sense, Adaptive Altruism proposes that under severe environmental stress, specialized cellular states may transiently emerge to preserve the organizational continuity of a complex adaptive biological system. Within this framework, transient cooperative behaviours—including niche modulation, cytoprotection, stromal reprogramming, immune regulation, and stress-memory formation—are interpreted as adaptive mechanisms that contribute to the preservation and reconstruction of biological self-identity despite continual cellular turnover, injury, and environmental perturbation.

Within the Adaptive Altruism framework, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory provides a possible bridge between transient cellular adaptation and the long-term preservation of biological identity. We hypothesize that repeated cycles of altruistic stem-cell activation maintain the stem-cell niche in a state of organized adaptive disequilibrium (Figure 36, p 140) rather than allowing it to relax toward thermodynamic equilibrium. In this view, niche memory preserves not the persistence of individual altruistic stem cells, but the dynamic organization of the niche itself through sustained remodeling of extracellular matrix, vascular architecture, metabolic gradients, and intercellular signaling networks. Consequently, biological self-identity is proposed to emerge as a systems-level property of this adaptive disequilibrium, continuously regenerated through interactions among stem cells, their niche, and environmental stress rather than being encoded within any single cell population. 

Within this broader perspective, we speculate that the "force of disequilibrium" proposed in The Science Behind Squalene (2000) (Figure 36) may provide a conceptual foundation for understanding Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory. In that earlier work, biological identity was proposed to emerge from the capacity of living systems to maintain a state of organized adaptive disequilibrium rather than relax toward thermodynamic equilibrium. Extending this concept, we propose that Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory represents one possible biological mechanism through which this adaptive disequilibrium may be preserved within tissue stem-cell niches. Specifically, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory refers to the persistence of functional and structural changes within the stem-cell niche following the disappearance of transient altruistic stem cells. Importantly, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory may represent one possible biological mechanism through which organized adaptive disequilibrium may be preserved within tissue stem-cell niches for tissue specific self-identity. 

Viewed from this perspective, the "force of disequilibrium" proposed in The Science Behind Squalene may not simply maintain normal tissue identity but may also determine the trajectory by which adaptive biological systems transition toward alternative stable states under chronic environmental stress. Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory is proposed here as one possible biological mechanism through which these persistent adaptive states are established and maintained.

Under physiological conditions, this adaptive disequilibrium supports tissue regeneration and homeostasis (organizational integrity or self-identity ) during repeated environmental stress. Thus, rather than encoding the fate of individual cells, it preserves the functional and organizational state of the niche itself, enabling subsequent generations of stem cells to re-establish tissue homeostasis. 

However, persistent pathological stress may chronically stabilize maladaptive attractor states. In tuberculosis, repeated niche remodeling may favor long-term persistence of dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In cancer, continuous CSC-mediated activation of adaptive niche-defense mechanisms may progressively stabilize a tumor-specific adaptive state, thereby contributing to the emergence and maintenance of tumor self-identity.  More broadly, we speculate that chronic environmental pollution, toxic nutrition, and sustained metabolic stress may similarly hijack adaptive stem-cell niche memory, progressively disrupting normal organ-specific self-identity and facilitating the emergence of disease-specific adaptive states. Within this framework, progressive disorders such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), cirrhosis, fibrosis, or adipose tissue dysfunction may be viewed not simply as cumulative tissue injury, but as gradual transitions from physiological to maladaptive niche organization, reflecting progressive re-establishment of an alternative disease-specific self-identity.

At present, direct experimental evidence demonstrating long-term persistence of Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory is lacking. Several fundamental questions remain unresolved. It is not yet known whether adaptive altruistic states represent a general property of normal stem-cell niches or are restricted to specific biological contexts. The molecular mechanisms responsible for storing and transmitting stress memory require further investigation, as do the roles of epigenetic regulation, lineage plasticity, and spatial niche organization. Future studies employing lineage tracing, single-cell multiomics, spatial transcriptomics, functional perturbation experiments, and longitudinal in vivo stress models and functional analyses of niche remodeling will be required to determine whether transient altruistic stem-cell responses generate persistent niche-level memory during regeneration, infection, or cancer.

Adaptive Altruism does not propose that cooperation replaces competition in biology. Rather, it proposes that the preservation of biological self-identity under stress requires transient, adaptive cooperation between specialized cellular states and their surrounding microenvironment, operating alongside competition within a complex adaptive system.

 

What the book said about cancer, and what changed

Chapter 5 presents cancer within the clonal evolution framework, as was standard at the time and as I then believed. Cancer is described as developing in a single cell through a process of evolution, with each division conferring further survival advantage, and the chapter states plainly that even cancer obeys the Darwinian law of natural selection. The framework I have developed since — in which a tumour behaves as an organized system that maintains and restores its composition — departs from that position. This commentary would be misleading if it presented the two as continuous.

The question that eventually produced that departure did not arise from the cancer biology literature. It arose from a rural oncology practice that came into existence almost by accident. In 1994 I was a newly qualified MBBS doctor. I had spent the preceding six months at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi, accompanying my father through chemotherapy and radiation for oesophageal cancer, and in the process had learned to administer cisplatin- and paclitaxel-based regimens. When we returned to our village in Kamrup district, villagers began asking whether I could give chemotherapy locally. Jagat Ghora — a Jiva Upakara Cikitsha healer, and one of my father's closest friends — had for years received cancer patients from across Assam for herbal treatment. He offered more than fifty of them to me as a starting cohort. Most had head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; the remainder had colon, ovarian, oesophageal, gall bladder cancer or leukaemia. Within a few months I had become proficient at delivering chemotherapy, and the practice that would eventually become KaviKrishna Telemedicine Care had begun. It was through Jagat Ghora and his patients that I encountered a tradition in which malignant disease was described as granthi — a knot, or organized entity, rather than a disordered mass. The designation was not applied to every tumour: a swelling became granthi only when judged to have acquired coherence as an entity, a state the healers associated with ahamkara, the principle of individuation and self-identity. Disease in this tradition was understood not simply as destruction but as a stressed living system acting to preserve itself.

Alongside the chemotherapy, I continued the dietary component of Jagat Ghora's practice, which included dattha xak — amaranth, among the richest plant sources of squalene. Patients reported fewer side effects. Whether that impression would have survived a controlled comparison I cannot say; it was an uncontrolled observation in an uncontrolled setting. But it was the observation that redirected my attention. The question it raised was not whether a plant helped, but whether an agent could exist that protected normal tissue from platinum toxicity without also protecting the tumour — and if so, what property would make such discrimination possible. That question, carried subsequently to Mongar Hospital in Bhutan, is the question this book was written to answer.

The concept of tumor as a granthi was something I ignored. Clonal evolution made great sense.

At the time this did not seem to me to bear on the biology, and I did not pursue it. That changed with experimental results published in 2008 showing that hypoxia enhances tumour stemness by expanding an invasive and tumorigenic side-population fraction — a finding that sat awkwardly within a purely selective account, since the stem-like fraction was being induced by the microenvironment rather than selected from standing variation. Returning to the earlier observation, and following it as a supposition to be tested rather than a claim to be accepted, I asked what cellular mechanisms could in principle allow a tumour to behave as a coherent self-preserving system, and why such behaviour would arise in some tumours and not others.

The origin of a hypothesis carries no evidential weight. This account motivated the question; everything that followed rests on experimental evidence. Its value here is that it contains a distinction current models of tumour adaptation do not make. Clonal evolution, stochastic plasticity and ecological frameworks describe adaptation as a continuous process operating in all tumours, and therefore treat aggressiveness as a matter of degree. They offer no account of a tumour becoming an organized entity, and no criterion separating those that do from those that do not.

 

An unnoticed thread: efflux pumps and the cancer stem cell phenotype

One continuity between the book and the subsequent experimental work went unremarked for many years. Chapter 5 sets out the requirements for a cytoprotective agent: it must discriminate a normal cell from a cancer cell and protect the former but not the latter — described there, in the first use of the term anywhere in this programme, as a kind of altruism or group fitness. The chapter then specifies how such selectivity might be achieved, identifying the efflux mechanism by which cancer cells pump out anticancer drugs as the property that distinguishes them from normal cells and therefore as the key to selective action.

Efflux subsequently became the operational basis of the entire experimental programme. The side-population phenotype is defined by dye efflux; ABCG2 is the transporter responsible; and EpCAM⁺/ABCG2⁺ sorting has been the method by which cancer stem cells were identified in every study from 2008 onward. The molecule named in 2000 as the thing that makes cancer cells different became the marker used to define the cells that mattered.

In the later work it denotes a cell-biological behaviour, in which a transient stem-cell state protects its neighbours and then eliminates itself. The word was retained; its referent changed.

Dr. Das and I had spoken at length about the Vedic altruism he learned from his father, and how it inspired him to study anti-oxidants and the cytoprotection of cells. Rather than "cytoprotection," he preferred the term "altruism" — not a word that fits readily into a book of hard science. I concurred with Dr. Bounous and he went with the more conventional term. It arises under conditions of severe stress, acts to restore the intrinsic balance of the individual or the community, and disappears once that task is complete. It is thus transient by definition: not a standing structure but a state that emerges, performs a protective function, and resolves.

These three properties — latency until stress, restoration of balance, and self-elimination on completion — correspond closely to what was later characterized experimentally as the altruistic stem cell and the Tumor Stemness Defense phenotype: a transient reprogrammed state, sustained for a bounded period, that secretes cytoprotective factors before undergoing apoptosis or differentiation. Whether this correspondence is more than structural resemblance is a question the tradition cannot answer and the experiments can. What can be said is that the concept supplied the expectation that a protective state should be temporary, and that its termination should be as characteristic of it as its induction — an expectation that shaped how the 2012 and subsequent experiments were designed and read.

The removal of this material from the 2000 text is the reason the conceptual line running from the tradition to the later work is not visible in the book itself, and has had to be documented separately.

titles.title: The Science Behind Squalene: The Human Antioxidant (The Conceptual Source of Stem Cell Niche Defense and Adaptive Altruism Research)

descriptions.description:
Squalene is an isoprenoid antioxidant present in human skin, and a precursor of cholesterol. Squalene is an ancient antioxidant that layers the cell membranes of primitive life form such as archea and cynobacteria. Twenty six years ago, I focussed on Squalene metabolism, as I was interested in primitive oxidative stress and cancer. Initially, a draft on oxidative stress and cancer, written during my clinical practice in Assam and Bhutan during 1994-1998, and as a part of my first research project, the project evolved rapidly during 1999-2000, when Mr. Dieter Beer proposed to write a book on Squalene dietary supplement to expand the dietary supplement markets. I took that opportunity and funding to make an indepth review on adaptive mechanisms against oxidative stress and metabolic stress. 

First published in August 2000, The Science Behind Squalene was not fundamentally a book about squalene; it was an investigation into whether evolutionarily conserved anti-oxidant metabolic networks constitute the first adaptive defense mechanisms by which living systems preserve biological organization under environmental stress.

The monograph outlines the biophysical, cellular and evolutionary foundations of squalene as an endogenous isoprenoid antioxidant. Its "Force of Disequilibrium" U-tube model (Figure 36, p. 140) provides an early theoretical framework for how living systems expend energy continuously to maintain non-equilibrium steady states rather than relaxing toward equilibrium. The chapter "Metabolic Stress and Chaos" proposed that antioxidant defense operates through nonlinear adaptive mechanisms maintaining an organized state of disequilibrium until critical stress thresholds are exceeded, beyond which the compensatory mechanism fails through positive feedback. Written before complex adaptive systems became widely applied in systems biology, this framework anticipated concepts now associated with resilience, nonlinear dynamics, threshold behaviour and adaptive biological organization.

Figure 14 (p. 52) presents the evolution of immune defense from ancestral stem cells under evolutionary pressure; the stem-cell niche-defense reading of this material developed subsequently.

A single clause on p. 12 notes that amaranth is a symbol of avatar kosha in tantric tradition — the only trace in the published text of a larger body of material on Vedic Jiva Upakara Cikitsha Tantra (https://doi.org/10.5040/9798216171232.0007) that was removed before publication.

Together, these early models established the biophysical and heuristic foundation for what later evolved over a 25-year research program into Stem Cell Niche Defense, Altruistic Stem Cells (ASCs), Tumor Stemness Defense (TSD), and the broader systems-biology framework of Adaptive Altruism.

Inspired by the Avatar Kosha of Vedic Altruism, Adaptive Altruism is proposed as a biological theory of transient enhanced-fitness altruism of stem cell niche defense. It is defined as a non-genetic stress-response program wherein actor stem cells utilize an active force of disequilibrium to initially gain metabolic fitness and robustness, execute collective niche protection from a position of strength, and subsequently undergo terminal self-elimination (Adaptive Altruism: scientific translation of Vedic Altruism, p. 11. https://zenodo.org/records/8062404). Beyond immediate cytoprotection, the adaptive-altruistic episode may generate persistent biological information that contributes to the emergence, maintenance, or reconstruction of biological self-identity.

The book should therefore be read not simply as a monograph on squalene, but as an early conceptual foundation for later work investigating how complex adaptive biological systems preserve and reconstruct their organizational identity under stress.

 

Commentary on the book: 

(During the twenty-sixth anniversary of The Science Behind Squalene, a commemorative lecture entitled "From Stem Cell Altruism to Tumor Self-Identity: Rethinking Cancer as a Cooperative System" was delivered at Assam DownTown University in February 2026. Preparing that lecture prompted a comprehensive re-examination of nearly three decades of clinical observations, experimental investigations, and conceptual development, and a need to write a commentary about this book, especially the last chapter, Metabolic Stress and Chaos.  This realization provided the immediate motivation to write a commentary on the book. This is the concept note of the future commentary)

Twenty-Six Years Later: From Adaptive Mechanism of Metabolic Stress  Response to Adaptive Altruism

When The Science Behind Squalene was first published in 2000, it was presented as a scientific exploration of squalene biology, antioxidant defense, metabolic stress, and environmental adaptation. Although centered on a naturally occurring isoprenoid molecule, the book was never intended to be merely a discussion of nutritional supplementation. Rather, it sought to address a broader biological question that had emerged from earlier clinical observations in community oncology: How do living systems preserve themselves under conditions of stress?

Looking back twenty-six years later, it has become apparent that many of the concepts introduced in the book—including adaptive metabolic mechanisms, organized disequilibrium, nonlinear biological organization, stress thresholds, evolutionary adaptation, and endogenous defense systems—represented the earliest formulation of a research programme that subsequently expanded far beyond antioxidant biology. Over the following decades, experimental investigations in hypoxia, stem-cell biology, cancer stem cells, mesenchymal stromal cells, host–pathogen interactions, and tumor microenvironment research progressively transformed these initial concepts into the hypotheses of Stem Cell Niche Defense, the Tumor Stemness Switch, Altruistic Stem Cells, Tumor Stemness Defense, and, most recently, Adaptive Altruism.

This commentary does not seek to reinterpret the original book through hindsight or to claim that later discoveries were already established in 2000. On the contrary, the original text is preserved exactly as it was written. The purpose of the present commentary is to place the book within its historical scientific context by explaining how its central questions evolved through subsequent experimental investigation. Where appropriate, annotations identify concepts that were later supported experimentally, concepts that evolved into new hypotheses, and ideas that remain speculative and require further validation.

 Revisiting the book in light of nearly three decades of research revealed that apparently diverse studies—including antioxidant metabolism, oxidative stress, hypoxia, stem-cell biology, tumor stemness, mesenchymal stromal cell reprogramming, microbial persistence, and community oncology—were not isolated investigations, but successive stages of a single evolving scientific programme. Each addressed different aspects of one overarching systems-level question: How do complex adaptive systems preserve and reconstruct their organizational self-identity under condition of stress?

Adaptive Altruism is proposed as one experimentally grounded, yet still evolving, framework through which this question can now be investigated.

Seen from this perspective, The Science Behind Squalene can be understood as the first conceptual foundation of that programme. The focus of the book was adaptive metabolism; subsequent work expanded this framework to stem-cell biology, tumor biology, and systems medicine. The central scientific question, however, remained remarkably consistent.

Adaptive Altruism, as discussed below and elsewhere, should therefore be regarded not as a departure from the ideas presented in the book, but as their current conceptual synthesis based on twenty-five years of additional experimental evidence.

This commentary is offered in the spirit of scientific continuity. It documents the evolution of ideas rather than their finality, distinguishing historical inspiration from experimental evidence, and established observations from hypothesis-driven interpretation. It is hoped that these annotations will help readers appreciate not only the historical significance of the original book, but also the iterative nature of scientific discovery, in which clinical observation, conceptual reasoning, experimental investigation, and continual revision together shape the emergence of new scientific frameworks.

Adaptive Altruism and the Preservation of Self-Identity in Complex Adaptive Systems

One of the central ideas emerging from The Science Behind Squalene was that biological stress does not arise simply from exposure to environmental injury, but from the failure of adaptive mechanisms responsible for maintaining an organized state of biological disequilibrium. The book proposed that antioxidant defense represents a dynamic, nonlinear process in which living systems continuously adjust their metabolic organization to preserve function under changing environmental conditions. Concepts such as adaptive metabolic responses, organized disequilibrium, stress thresholds, and nonlinear biological organization anticipated a systems-level view of biological resilience, although the terminology of "complex adaptive systems" was not employed at that time.

Over the subsequent twenty-five years, experimental investigations progressively expanded this conceptual framework from metabolism to stem-cell biology, cancer biology, and host-pathogen interactions. Studies of hypoxia revealed that severe stress induces transient stemness through MYC-HIF-2α signalling, enabling subsets of stem cells and cancer stem cells to enter reversible stress-adaptive states. Subsequent work identified altruistic stem cells (ASCs) capable of protecting neighbouring cells through cytoprotective secretory programmes in the lung and BM niches, while later studies demonstrated that tumour-derived signals reprogram mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into Mesenchymal Altruistic Stem Cells (M-ASCs), establishing stem cell niche memory within the tumour microenvironment. More recently, the Tumor Stemness Defense (TSD) phenotype was proposed to explain how hypoxic cancer stem cells (CSCs) may transiently adopt niche-supportive functions that preserve dormant cancer stem-cell reservoirs and facilitate tumour recurrence through the CSC reawakening process. Collectively, these findings support the broader concept that stress adaptation is not exclusively cell-autonomous but may involve transient cooperative interactions that preserve the organization of the larger cellular ecosystem.

These experimental observations have led to the formulation of Adaptive Altruism as a systems-level hypothesis. Rather than describing altruism in the classical evolutionary sense, Adaptive Altruism proposes that under severe environmental stress, specialized cellular states may transiently emerge to preserve the organizational continuity of a complex adaptive biological system. Within this framework, transient cooperative behaviours—including niche modulation, cytoprotection, stromal reprogramming, immune regulation, and stress-memory formation—are interpreted as adaptive mechanisms that contribute to the preservation and reconstruction of biological self-identity despite continual cellular turnover, injury, and environmental perturbation.

Within the Adaptive Altruism framework, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory provides a possible bridge between transient cellular adaptation and the long-term preservation of biological identity. We hypothesize that repeated cycles of altruistic stem-cell activation maintain the stem-cell niche in a state of organized adaptive disequilibrium (Figure 36, p 140) rather than allowing it to relax toward thermodynamic equilibrium. In this view, niche memory preserves not the persistence of individual altruistic stem cells, but the dynamic organization of the niche itself through sustained remodeling of extracellular matrix, vascular architecture, metabolic gradients, and intercellular signaling networks. Consequently, biological self-identity is proposed to emerge as a systems-level property of this adaptive disequilibrium, continuously regenerated through interactions among stem cells, their niche, and environmental stress rather than being encoded within any single cell population. 

Within this broader perspective, we speculate that the "force of disequilibrium" proposed in The Science Behind Squalene (2000) (Figure 36) may provide a conceptual foundation for understanding Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory. In that earlier work, biological identity was proposed to emerge from the capacity of living systems to maintain a state of organized adaptive disequilibrium rather than relax toward thermodynamic equilibrium. Extending this concept, we propose that Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory represents one possible biological mechanism through which this adaptive disequilibrium may be preserved within tissue stem-cell niches. Specifically, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory refers to the persistence of functional and structural changes within the stem-cell niche following the disappearance of transient altruistic stem cells. Importantly, Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory may represent one possible biological mechanism through which organized adaptive disequilibrium may be preserved within tissue stem-cell niches for tissue specific self-identity. 

Viewed from this perspective, the "force of disequilibrium" proposed in The Science Behind Squalene may not simply maintain normal tissue identity but may also determine the trajectory by which adaptive biological systems transition toward alternative stable states under chronic environmental stress. Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory is proposed here as one possible biological mechanism through which these persistent adaptive states are established and maintained.

Under physiological conditions, this adaptive disequilibrium supports tissue regeneration and homeostasis (organizational integrity or self-identity ) during repeated environmental stress. Thus, rather than encoding the fate of individual cells, it preserves the functional and organizational state of the niche itself, enabling subsequent generations of stem cells to re-establish tissue homeostasis. 

However, persistent pathological stress may chronically stabilize maladaptive attractor states. In tuberculosis, repeated niche remodeling may favor long-term persistence of dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In cancer, continuous CSC-mediated activation of adaptive niche-defense mechanisms may progressively stabilize a tumor-specific adaptive state, thereby contributing to the emergence and maintenance of tumor self-identity.  More broadly, we speculate that chronic environmental pollution, toxic nutrition, and sustained metabolic stress may similarly hijack adaptive stem-cell niche memory, progressively disrupting normal organ-specific self-identity and facilitating the emergence of disease-specific adaptive states. Within this framework, progressive disorders such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), cirrhosis, fibrosis, or adipose tissue dysfunction may be viewed not simply as cumulative tissue injury, but as gradual transitions from physiological to maladaptive niche organization, reflecting progressive re-establishment of an alternative disease-specific self-identity.

At present, direct experimental evidence demonstrating long-term persistence of Adaptive Stem Cell Niche Memory is lacking. Several fundamental questions remain unresolved. It is not yet known whether adaptive altruistic states represent a general property of normal stem-cell niches or are restricted to specific biological contexts. The molecular mechanisms responsible for storing and transmitting stress memory require further investigation, as do the roles of epigenetic regulation, lineage plasticity, and spatial niche organization. Future studies employing lineage tracing, single-cell multiomics, spatial transcriptomics, functional perturbation experiments, and longitudinal in vivo stress models and functional analyses of niche remodeling will be required to determine whether transient altruistic stem-cell responses generate persistent niche-level memory during regeneration, infection, or cancer.

Adaptive Altruism does not propose that cooperation replaces competition in biology. Rather, it proposes that the preservation of biological self-identity under stress requires transient, adaptive cooperation between specialized cellular states and their surrounding microenvironment, operating alongside competition within a complex adaptive system.

titles.title: Towards Trustworthy Biological Alignment in TabPFN-Probed Pathology Foundation Models

descriptions.description: Histology and transcriptomics provide complementary views of tissue biology, capturing spatial morphology and molecular activity, respectively. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) learn rich morphological representations from H&E images, yet strong downstream performance alone does not establish whether these representations encode biologically meaningful and robust molecular information. We present a **training-free framework for auditing biological alignment in frozen PFMs** using spatially paired histology and transcriptomics from HEST-1k, evaluated on **240 samples spanning three organs**. Multiple frozen PFMs are used to extract H&E representations, while gene expression is aggregated into biologically interpretable pathway-level programs. We use TabPFN as a pretrained probe to quantify the extent to which these molecular programs can be decoded from frozen image representations without task-specific gradient updates. Beyond predictive performance, our audit examines whether pathway decodability generalizes across tissue sections, patient groups, and tissue types; whether representations exhibit section-level or other shortcut dependencies; and whether predictions remain stable under small image perturbations and context resampling. This multi-tissue evaluation distinguishes molecular programs that are consistently encoded from those that are tissue-specific, unstable, or shortcut-sensitive. Our framework therefore provides a systematic approach for assessing not only **what biological information pathology foundation models encode, but also how reliably that information persists under clinically relevant sources of variation**.

titles.title: SpaFactor: Lightweight Spatial Context-Aware Gene Program Modeling for Histology-to-Transcriptomics Inference

descriptions.description: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) profiles gene expression within tissue architecture, but its cost and experimental complexity limit routine use. Predicting spatial expression from routinely available hematoxylin and eosin (HE) images therefore offers a scalable alternative. However, conventional methods often fit high-dimensional gene outputs as independent targets, overlooking the biological coordination among genes while remaining vulnerable to high-dimensional noise and overfitting. Existing attempts to address this limitation often rely on computationally heavy graph networks or complex auxiliary supervision. We therefore introduce SpaFactor, a lightweight and efficient low-rank morphology-program-gene factorization framework. At the input, SpaFactor efficiently fuses the visual representation of the central spot with multiscale local and regional neighborhood context, yielding a histologic representation that captures cellular morphology and microenvironmental heterogeneity. For modeling, a residual MLP stably learns a nonlinear mapping from the tissue microenvironment to low-dimensional latent gene programs. These activities are decoded through shared gene loadings into coordinated multi-gene expression predictions. Across five public cohorts, SpaFactor achieves the best aggregate performance, with particularly clear improvements for spatially variable genes, and more faithfully recovers biologically organized spatial patterns. These results demonstrate that lightweight joint modeling of tissue context and gene programs can improve both predictive accuracy and biological fidelity.

titles.title: Spatial MALDI-Visium data from mouse hippocampus

descriptions.description: This dataset contains paired spatial metabolomics and spatial transcriptomics data from two mouse hippocampus tissue sections used in the COSIE study. Each section includes spatial MALDI measurements and 10x Genomics Visium gene-expression data.

titles.title: Spatial MALDI-Visium data from mouse hippocampus

descriptions.description: This dataset contains paired spatial metabolomics and spatial transcriptomics data from two mouse hippocampus tissue sections used in the COSIE study. Each section includes spatial MALDI measurements and 10x Genomics Visium gene-expression data.

The SCAPeSCLC Reproducible R Workflows contain the R scripts used for the curation, harmonization, analysis, and expansion of the SCAPeSCLC dataset (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.19897644). These workflows reproduce the analytical pipeline used to generate the processed data products, survival analyses, and diagnostic atlases distributed with the dataset. SCAPeSCLC is a harmonized, multi-level transcriptomic and clinical resource integrating region-of-interest (ROI)- and patient-level molecular profiles with standardized clinical annotations, survival outcomes, Bayesian pathway activity estimates, and comprehensive survival analysis outputs into a unified analytical framework for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC).

The SCAPeSCLC Reproducible R Workflows contain the R scripts used for the curation, harmonization, analysis, and expansion of the SCAPeSCLC dataset (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.19897644). These workflows reproduce the analytical pipeline used to generate the processed data products, survival analyses, and diagnostic atlases distributed with the dataset. SCAPeSCLC is a harmonized, multi-level transcriptomic and clinical resource integrating region-of-interest (ROI)- and patient-level molecular profiles with standardized clinical annotations, survival outcomes, Bayesian pathway activity estimates, and comprehensive survival analysis outputs into a unified analytical framework for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC).

Added 04_SCAPeSCLC_diagnostic_atlas_generator_for_genes_confounder_adjusted.R for automated generation of confounder-adjusted gene-level diagnostic atlases incorporating treatment and bone metastasis as adjustment variables while reporting gene-specific hazard ratio estimates.
